questions.prompt: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?

options.text: HAVING filters rows before grouping; WHERE filters after
They are interchangeable in all queries
WHERE works only on numeric columns
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation

questions.explanation: WHERE is applied to individual rows before GROUP BY, so it cannot reference aggregates. HAVING is applied to the groups produced by GROUP BY, so it can.

questions.prompt: Consider a table T with 10 rows, where the column C has 3 NULLs and 7 non-NULL values (2 of them duplicates). What does SELECT COUNT(C) FROM T return?
questions.explanation: COUNT(column) ignores NULLs, giving 7. COUNT(*) would return 10, and COUNT(DISTINCT C) would exclude duplicates as well.

questions.prompt: Which JOIN returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where no match exists on the right?
questions.explanation: A LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves every row of the left relation, padding the right side with NULLs when the join condition finds no match.

questions.prompt: In SQL, the expression (NULL = NULL) evaluates to:
questions.explanation: SQL uses three-valued logic. Any comparison involving NULL yields UNKNOWN, which is why IS NULL exists — rows where the predicate is UNKNOWN are not returned by WHERE.

questions.prompt: Which clause is evaluated LAST in a standard SQL SELECT query?
questions.explanation: Logical evaluation order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, then ORDER BY. Because ORDER BY runs after SELECT, it can reference column aliases defined there.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the DISTINCT keyword in SELECT DISTINCT A, B FROM T?

options.text: Removes duplicates from column A only
Sorts the result by A then B
Removes rows where the combination (A, B) is duplicated

questions.explanation: DISTINCT applies to the entire projected row, so duplicate (A, B) pairs collapse to one. It does not apply per column, and it does not sort.

questions.prompt: Which SQL statement removes all rows from a table but keeps the table structure, and cannot be rolled back in many systems because it is not fully logged?
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE is a DDL operation that deallocates data pages wholesale. DELETE is DML, logs each row and can be rolled back; DROP removes the table definition entirely.

questions.prompt: A table Employee(eid, name, dept) has 12 rows across 4 departments. How many rows does SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Employee GROUP BY dept return?
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses the rows into one output row per distinct grouping value, so 4 departments give 4 rows, each with its own count.

questions.prompt: Which constraint guarantees that a column's values are unique but, unlike a primary key, permits a NULL?
questions.explanation: UNIQUE enforces distinctness while generally allowing NULLs (which are not considered equal to one another). A PRIMARY KEY is effectively UNIQUE plus NOT NULL.

questions.prompt: What does a correlated subquery do that an ordinary subquery does not?

options.text: It references columns from the outer query, so it is re-evaluated per outer row
It always executes faster than a join
It returns multiple columns by definition
It can only appear in the FROM clause

questions.explanation: A correlated subquery depends on the current outer row, so conceptually it runs once per outer row. That dependency is exactly why it is often slower than an equivalent join.
